title: Use AI to Build Fireplaces
author: Josh Brake
summary: Josh Brake, an engineering professor, describes how generative AI has reshaped his work this semester as he co-teaches a new course on building AI-powered apps. He and his co-instructor use Claude to adapt materials, build lab notebooks and in-class activities, and make diagrams and quizzes, while students may use AI only through a custom platform that tutors without giving answers. Assessment pairs weekly labs with 15-minute oral check-ins and handwritten quizzes, which removes the incentive to rush through the labs. He then draws on Albert Borgmann's device paradigm, contrasting a fireplace, which gathers a household, with a furnace, which only produces heat efficiently. His claim is that AI can either commoditize one dimension of teaching or help build more embodied, human learning experiences, and educators should aim at fireplaces.
points: AI let the instructors extend existing expertise to build tailored labs, activities and quizzes far faster, freeing time for conversation with students.
Rather than banning AI or leaving it open, the course prescribes use through a custom tutoring platform designed to deepen understanding without giving away answers.
Weekly oral check-ins and handwritten quizzes make AI-assisted labs a preparation for demonstrated understanding rather than a finished product.
Borgmann's fireplace versus furnace contrast frames the choice between commoditizing one measurable output and creating focal practices that gather people.
Generative AI did not create the narrow, instrumental view of education; it accelerated it, so the response is creativity in design rather than resignation or dismissal.
quotes: It has enabled me to create materials to engage my students in more active, experiential learning. It has allowed me to extend my expertise as an educator and become a better one.
But instead of prohibiting AI or having an open AI policy, we’ve carefully prescribed the way that they interact with AI to help maximize the alignment between their AI use and their learning.
Each week they complete a scaffolded lab assignment, but completing the lab is only used to preparation for a 15-minute oral check in with an instructor each week.

Claude has enabled us to extend our pre-existing expertise to create tailored learning materials much more rapidly than we would have been able to otherwise, executing on our ideas more quickly and freeing us up to be more creative and to spend more time in conversation with the students in the course.
Seen from the perspective of producing heat, a fireplace and a furnace are doing the same thing. But the fireplace creates a certain environment within a home.

Do we want to use it to create ever more efficient ways to commoditize a specific aspect of our work, making it easier, cheaper, faster to create? Or do we want to use it to create more effective fireplaces?

The default may indeed be for generative AI to encourage our students to develop a narrower and instrumental view of their education. But generative AI didn’t create that problem, it simply accelerated the endgame.
Whether we use generative AI or not, let’s focus on making fireplaces that encourage focal practices, not furnaces that undermine the very conditions needed for them to exist at all.
